Under the three rules the owner named (R1, R2, R3) the four current slots receive identical reserves, but at least one other deterministic, result-blind rule (descending selection index) pairs them differently and moves a different reserve into FINAL_HOLDOUT. sd9.r3Rule8Verbatim: An organisation is ACQUISITION_SUCCESSFUL iff, after policy-authorised discovery and after SD7 deduplication, it yields at least MIN_PAGES_PER_ORGANISATION = 4 distinct pages with extractable text. Acquisition per organisation is bounded by the already frozen Phase 2B-1e orchestrator budgets and acquires at most MAX_PAGES_ACQUIRED_PER_ORGANISATION = 35 ordinary pages. Acquisition STOPS when 110 ACQUISITION_SUCCESSFUL organisations exist, or when the reserve list is exhausted - in which case the freeze is REFUSED.

replacementRule.r3Verbatim: If an organisation on the selection list is NOT ACQUISITION_SUCCESSFUL (SD9), it is replaced by the next unused RESERVE organisation in rank order, and the replacement INHERITS the replaced organisation selection index and therefore its split. Every replacement is recorded with both eche_row_keys and the reason. This keeps 20 / 45 / 45 exact and keeps the split assignment independent of acquisition outcome.
replacementRule.planVerbatim: A selected organisation that is not ACQUISITION_SUCCESSFUL is replaced by the next unused RESERVE organisation in rank order; the replacement inherits the replaced organisation's selection index and therefore its split. No reshuffle.

reserveExhaustion.r3Verbatim: If the reserve is exhausted before 110 successful organisations exist, the corpus freeze is REFUSED. A smaller corpus is never silently accepted, because every denominator in section D depends on the count.

section3_p5Purpose.question: Is P5 a permanent stop of Generation 1 (A), or a batch safety barrier that requires human review before a new bounded live window may be authorised (B)?

proof.argument: R3 names exactly two conditions under which acquisition stops: 110 ACQUISITION_SUCCESSFUL organisations, or reserve exhaustion (freeze REFUSED). P5 is neither. Reading P5 as a permanent Generation-1 stop would add a third stop condition that the frozen methodology does not contain, and would leave Generation 1 at 5 successes with 40 unused reserves - a state R3 classifies as neither complete nor refused.

verbatim: a systematic defect would consume all 150 organisations of live contact before anyone looked
how much live institution contact happens before a human inspects the result - approximately 5 x 60 = 300 requests
proof.argument: The stated purpose of batching, and therefore of batch-level pause conditions, is that a human inspects before more live contact. That purpose is satisfied by inspection, not by permanent cessation.

proof.verbatim: > 30% of a batch fails the SD9 >= 4-page minimum
proof.argument: The denominator is a batch. A cohort-wide reading has no denominator in this text.

proof.verbatim: record the batch boundary, the reason and the replacement-ledger state, and stop. Never degrade, retry with different settings, or continue with a widened budget.
proof.argument: The plan expects a pause to leave a batch BOUNDARY and a replacement-ledger STATE - both presuppose later batches and ongoing replacement. The prohibitions are on degrading, re-trying differently and widening, not on a new, identically-bounded, separately-authorised window.

proof.verbatim: The response to a genuine refusal is to consume a reserve organisation, never to retry differently.
proof.argument: The plan's own answer to legitimate acquisition failure is the replacement mechanism, which requires further live acquisition.

section16_replacementChain.question: If the reserve replacing slot 3 is itself ACQUISITION_UNSUCCESSFUL, does the next unused reserve replace the same slot again?
section16_replacementChain.answer: YES - mechanically implied, not literally stated
section16_replacementChain.argument: R3's stop conditions are exhaustive: 110 successes, or reserve exhaustion. A slot left holding a failed occupant, with reserves unused, is neither. The only frozen mechanism that moves a slot toward success is replacement, and the replacement 'INHERITS the replaced organisation selection index', so it is the slot's occupant and is subject to the same rule. A narrow literal reading ('on the selection list' = the original 110 only) would make 110 unreachable while reserves remain, contradicting R3's own stop rule.

section16_replacementChain.withinTheProposedWindow: Does not arise dynamically: the window's five items are precommitted, so a failed replacement re-opens its slot for a LATER window's assignment, in R1 order among all slots then awaiting.

section17_terminology.ACQUISITION_OF_RECORD: per ORGANISATION: which of that organisation's runs the generation reads. Moved ONLY by the acquisition-policy transition ledger, token SUPERSEDED_FOR_GENERATION_ACQUISITION_DECISION_BY_POLICY_REPAIR.
section17_terminology.SLOT_OCCUPANT: per SELECTION INDEX: which organisation currently holds that index. The ORIGINAL_OCCUPANT is the draw's selection entry; a REPLACEMENT_OCCUPANT is set ONLY by the reserve replacement ledger.
section17_terminology.REPLACED_OUT_OCCUPANT: an organisation that has left a slot. Its runs, observations and acquisition of record stay immutable evidence; it is never deleted, never marked erroneous, and never 'superseded'.
section17_terminology.slotStatus: derived: the SD9 status of the current occupant's acquisition of record - SUCCESS | FAILURE_AWAITING_REPLACEMENT | OCCUPANT_NEVER_STARTED | PENDING_SD7
section17_terminology.neverConflate: Replacement is not supersession. Supersession changes which RUN of the same organisation counts; replacement changes which ORGANISATION holds the slot. They live in different ledgers so that 'how many reserves are consumed?' is a row count, not a reason-column filter (V2/V3/V4 transition ledgers, thisIsNotTheReserveReplacementLedger).
